It's still fairly far removed from our current capabilities. Robots work very well at doing repetitive tasks but are awful when it comes to thinking creatively. Even the much-buzzed alpha-go was created by slamming deep learning networks against each other for thousands of hours until the program learned what worked and didn't. It's not an elegant process and the result is only narrowly applicable with the exact inputs the network developed around.

I guess what I'm trying to say is that it's exceedingly easy to purpose-build a robot-- to create a piece of equipment that will take well-controlled inputs and turn them into well-controlled outputs. The layer of complexity that we haven't even begun to start adding into the mix is handling broad ranges of inputs.

For an example, if a human repair man is sent into the field to repair a disabled autonomous inventory unit that crashed into a ditch, he can analyze the damage and situation completely and account for external factors that don't or aren't directly related to the damage to the vehicle. For instance, imagine if it crashed into a tree and the chassis over the electric motor were ripped loose. The engine is now covered in dirt and debris. It's trivial for a human to ignore the dirt and debris and work on fixing the underlying problem. Our current vision systems, however, might not even recognize that they're looking at an engine made out of the parts that the program knows should be there. Our brains are very good at processing the essential from the extraneous. This is something that vision systems (and AI in general) struggle with, largely because we don't even understand how or why our brains can.
